title: Berlin wisdom paradigm
aliases: wisdom as expertise in the fundamental pragmatics of life
summary: A research model, developed by Paul Baltes and colleagues in Berlin, that treats wisdom as expert knowledge and judgment about the conduct and meaning of life, measured by rating people's think-aloud answers to hard life dilemmas against five criteria.
selfCheck: Have I considered how this problem looks across the person's whole life, past and future, and not only today?
Have I named what I do not know about this situation, and what I would do if things turn out differently than I expect?
Am I judging this choice by my own values only, or have I tried to understand the values and priorities behind it?

title: Buddhism
summary: A religious and philosophical tradition that began with the teaching of Siddhārtha Gautama, the Buddha, in northern India around the fifth century BCE, which diagnoses suffering as arising from craving and ignorance and sets out a path of ethics, meditation and wisdom to bring it to an end.

title: Compassionate reappraisal
aliases: letting go of anger through compassion
summary: A short reflective exercise for someone who has wronged you: you keep the wrong in view but deliberately see the offender as a whole, flawed human being who needs to change, and try to wish them well, instead of replaying the hurt.
selfCheck: Am I wishing this person well, or am I telling myself that what they did was fine?
Is this wrong still going on and within my power to change, so that action rather than reappraisal is the priority?
After the exercise, what concrete step, if any, does fairness to me or others still require?
Am I trying this because I'm ready, or because I feel I ought to have moved on by now?
steps: Sit somewhere quiet and settle your breathing for a minute or two before you start.
Recall one specific time a particular person hurt or wronged you, and name plainly what they did and what it cost you.
Picture the offender as a whole person with a history, fears and other sides to them, not only as the author of this act.
Treat the wrong as a sign that this person needs to grow or change, without telling yourself it was acceptable.
Try, for about two minutes, to sincerely wish them something good, such as healing or becoming someone who would not do this again.
Notice your thoughts, feelings and body as you do this, and repeat the exercise when you catch yourself replaying the hurt.
Decide separately, on the facts, what boundary, conversation or accountability the situation still needs.

example.situation: A teammate missed a handover deadline and then told your manager the delay was your fault, and you lie awake replaying it.
example.before: I keep going over every word they said to the manager. They're two-faced, that's all there is to it, and I'll be cold to them from now on.
example.after: They were wrong to blame me, and I'll correct the record with the manager tomorrow. They were scared of being blamed, which doesn't excuse it, and I hope they learn to own their mistakes. I can wish them that and still watch my back.
example.why: Replaying the offence keeps anger and arousal high, while seeing the person as flawed and in need of change lets the anger ease without denying the wrong or giving up the practical response.

title: Deliberation
summary: The capacity to think a choice through before acting: working out, for something that is up to you and whose outcome is uncertain, which available course will best reach a worthwhile end, and then settling on it.
selfCheck: Is this decision actually within my power, and is the outcome really uncertain, or am I deliberating to put off accepting something?
Have I checked that the goal itself is a good one, not just how to reach it?
Did I consider more than one way forward before settling on the first idea I had?
Is my confidence here earned by long, well-fed-back experience, or is it just a strong feeling?
Have I set a point where thinking stops and acting starts?
steps: Check that the matter is actually up to you and that its outcome is genuinely uncertain; if not, stop deliberating and either accept it or act on what is known.
Say plainly what you are trying to achieve, and ask whether that end is worth pursuing before you plan how to reach it.
List at least two or three realistic ways of getting there, not just the first one that occurred to you.
For the most promising option, trace backwards from the goal to the very next thing you would have to do, and drop options whose chain hits something impossible.
If the decision is important, talk it through with someone who knows this kind of situation.
Before trusting a strong gut feeling, ask whether you have had long, well-fed-back experience with situations like this one.
Set a point at which deliberation ends, then choose and act promptly, without reopening the question unless new facts appear.

example.situation: A manager has to decide within a week whether to move a struggling analyst to a different team or keep coaching her in her current role.
example.before: My gut says she's not cut out for this. I'll announce the move on Monday and be done with it.
example.after: Is this really my call, and what am I trying to achieve: her success, or a quieter team? Let me list the options, including a coaching plan with a review date, talk it over with HR and her previous lead, and decide by Thursday.
example.why: The wiser response clarifies the goal, widens the options and borrows others' judgment on an important, uncertain matter, but still commits to a decision on time instead of drifting.

title: Forgiveness
summary: The settled readiness to give up resentment and the wish for revenge toward someone who wronged you, while still judging that what they did was wrong, without requiring that you forget, excuse or reconcile.
selfCheck: Am I holding on to this to protect myself or someone else, or mainly to make them pay?
Have I separated forgiving from excusing, forgetting and reconciling, so I know which of these I'm actually being asked to do?
If they keep doing this, what boundary would self-respect require alongside any forgiveness?
Have I given myself time to name the hurt before deciding whether, and how, to forgive?

example.situation: A colleague presented your analysis as their own to a client, later admitted it and apologised, and you still have to work together on the account.
example.before: I'll be polite, but I'm keeping score, and I'll make sure the client finds out what they're really like.
example.after: I'll tell them plainly that it was wrong and that I'll put my name on my own work from now on. Then I'll stop rehearsing it and treat them fairly on this project.
example.why: Forgiving here means dropping the campaign of payback while keeping the judgement that it was wrong and the safeguards that protect you; it is neither pretending nothing happened nor trusting blindly.

title: Gratitude
summary: The settled disposition to recognise goods you have received, to see that they came from the goodwill of someone else, and to respond with fitting thanks and goodwill in return, without servility or a ledger of debts.
selfCheck: Have I noticed who made this good thing possible, and the effort or intention it took them?
Have I actually told them, specifically, rather than only feeling it?
Is my thanks free, or am I acting out of a sense of debt, guilt or deference I don't really owe?
Am I using "be grateful" to talk myself, or someone else, out of a legitimate complaint?

example.situation: A teammate quietly stayed late to fix a broken data feed so your quarterly report could go out on time.
example.before: Good, it's fixed. That's their job anyway; on to the next thing.
example.after: I'll tell them specifically what their evening saved, mention it to our manager, and keep an eye out for a chance to help them in turn.
example.why: Gratitude notices both the benefit and the goodwill behind it, then answers with thanks and goodwill rather than taking it for granted or treating it as a debt to settle and forget.

title: Humble leadership
aliases: leading by modelling how to grow
summary: A way of leading in which the person in charge openly admits their own limits and mistakes, gives visible credit for others' strengths and contributions, and shows they are still learning, so that the team treats growth and honest uncertainty as normal.
selfCheck: When did I last tell my team, in so many words, that I was wrong about something?
Who did the real work on this result, and have the people above me heard their names?
Am I asking for input because I will use it, or to look open?
Does this situation call for listening and learning, or for a fast, clear decision that I can review with the team later?
steps: When you get something wrong or don't know the answer, say so plainly and early, and say what you will do about it.
Name specific contributions by specific people, in their hearing and when reporting upward; say "we" for shared wins and "I" for your own errors.
Ask the team for feedback on one concrete thing you did, listen without defending, and tell them later what you changed.
Let people with more expertise on a task teach you, in front of others if possible.
Keep making clear decisions; in a crisis or under tight deadlines, act first and invite reflection afterwards.
Check that the humility is believed, not read as a tactic, by keeping your private conduct consistent with what you say in meetings.

example.situation: A project lead's schedule for a product launch slips by three weeks, partly because she under-estimated the testing work, and an analyst on the team had flagged the risk early.
example.before: The vendors let us down and testing turned out harder than anyone could have predicted. We'll push harder.
example.after: I under-estimated testing, and Priya flagged it in March; I should have listened. Here's the revised plan. Priya, can you walk me through how you sized it so I get it right next time?
example.why: Owning the error, crediting the person who saw it and asking to learn from her makes it safe for others to raise risks early, and it fixes the estimating method rather than just the date.

title: Implicit theories of wisdom
summary: The ideas about what wisdom is, who is wise and how wisdom grows that ordinary people carry around, usually without having spelled them out; psychologists study them by asking laypeople to describe, rate or nominate wise people, and contrast them with the explicit theories built by researchers.
selfCheck: When I call someone wise, am I responding to their judgment and care for others, or mainly to their intelligence, confidence or age?
Whose advice am I about to rely on here, and what picture of wisdom made me choose them?
Would someone raised with a different idea of wisdom see this choice as wise, and what would they weigh that I am leaving out?

title: Intellectual humility
summary: The character trait of noticing and owning the limits of what you know and of how well you reason: admitting gaps and possible error to yourself and others, without either inflating your intellectual strengths or collapsing into self-doubt, because you care more about getting things right than about looking right.
selfCheck: Which part of my view have I actually checked, and which part am I only sure of?
What evidence or argument would change my mind here, and have I gone looking for it?
When I was shown a mistake just now, did I feel curiosity or did I feel attacked?
Am I underselling a strength I really do have, out of false modesty or fear of conflict?

example.situation: In a project review, a colleague points out that the sales forecast you built last month rests on an assumption you never checked.
example.before: The model is fine. The market just shifted; nobody could have seen that coming.
example.after: You're right, I didn't test that assumption. Let's rerun it with your figure and see how much the forecast moves. Thanks for catching it.
example.why: Owning the gap, rather than blaming circumstances or brushing it off, fixes the forecast, shows the team that errors can be raised safely, and treats the critic as an ally in getting it right.

title: Know thyself
summary: The ancient Greek maxim inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi, read first as a reminder of human limits and later, through Socrates and Plato, as a call to examine one's own character, beliefs and ignorance; modern psychology adds that this is best done with the help of other people's views.
selfCheck: What would someone who knows me well say about me here that I would rather not hear?
Am I judging myself by my intentions while others can only see my behaviour?
Have I mistaken a confident story about my motives for real knowledge of them?

example.situation: After a project review, a manager is told by two team members that her meetings run long because she rarely lets others finish a point.
example.before: That's not me. I know how I come across, and I'm a good listener.
example.after: I don't experience myself that way, but two people saw the same thing. I'll ask a colleague to watch the next meeting and tell me what they notice.
example.why: Self-views are least reliable on flattering or unflattering traits, so treating others' observations as evidence rather than an attack is how the maxim is actually followed.

title: Memento mori
summary: The deliberate, regular practice of remembering that you will die and do not know when, used not to dwell on death but to see more clearly what deserves your time, attention and care today.
selfCheck: If my time were shorter than I assume, would this still be worth my anger or effort?
Am I using the thought of death to clarify what matters, or to feed dread or reckless indulgence?
What would I want to have said or done for the people involved here?
steps: Pick a fixed cue for the reflection, such as waking up, a commute, or the last few minutes before sleep.
Bring to mind, concretely and in your own case, that your life will end and that you do not know when.
Look back over the last day or week and ask how you actually spent your time and attention.
Ask what you would regret leaving undone or unsaid, and whom you would think of first.
Choose one concrete action for today that reflects what matters, and let go of one petty grievance or craving.
Return your attention to the task in front of you; if the reflection leaves you more anxious than clear, shorten it or stop.

example.situation: You have spent a week stewing over a curt email from a colleague and are drafting a sharp reply late in the evening while your family is in the next room.
example.before: I'll send a reply that puts them in their place, then keep going through my inbox until midnight.
example.after: If my time were shorter than I assume, this exchange would not be worth another evening. I'll send a short, civil reply tomorrow and spend tonight with the people in the next room.
example.why: Remembering that time is limited and uncertain shifts attention from winning a minor status contest to the relationships and values you would actually want to have served.

title: Negative visualization
summary: A Stoic exercise of deliberately imagining that you could lose what you value, or that a setback could happen, so that you hold good things with more appreciation and meet misfortune with less shock.
selfCheck: Am I rehearsing a possible loss in order to prepare and appreciate, or am I just worrying?
After imagining this loss, did I come back to what I still have and what I can do now?
Which parts of the outcome I fear are actually up to me?
steps: Choose one thing you value and tend to take for granted, such as a relationship, your health, your job or an ordinary comfort.
Remind yourself plainly of its nature, starting small, for example that this mug can break and that the people you love are mortal.
For a minute or two, imagine concretely what your life would be like without it, or how it might never have come about.
Return to the present and notice that you do still have it; name one way you will use or appreciate it today.
Before a risky plan, list what could go wrong, separate what is up to you from what is not, and prepare for the parts you can influence.
Stop if the exercise turns into dread or repetitive worry, and shorten it or set it aside.

example.situation: Your manager asks you to present to senior leadership next week, and you also have a job you mostly enjoy but have started to complain about.
example.before: I'll keep replaying how badly the presentation could go every night until then, and keep grumbling about this job.
example.after: Once, I'll list what could go wrong in the presentation, prepare for the questions I can foresee, and accept that the reaction isn't fully up to me. And I'll take a minute to picture not having this job at all, then notice what I'd miss.
example.why: A brief, bounded rehearsal turns vague fear into preparation and restores appreciation, whereas dwelling on the worst only adds suffering before anything has happened.

title: Post-traumatic growth
summary: Positive psychological change that people report after struggling with a highly challenging life event, such as deeper relationships, a stronger sense of personal strength or a greater appreciation of life. How often such reports reflect real change, rather than a hopeful story told afterwards, is disputed.

title: Purpose in life
summary: A lasting, central aim that organises a person's goals and daily choices, feels personally meaningful and, on most accounts, reaches beyond the self; psychologists treat it as one facet of meaning in life and a predictor, though not a proven cause, of better health and longer survival.

title: Robert J. Sternberg
summary: American psychologist (Yale, Tufts, Oklahoma State, Cornell) best known for his work on intelligence, creativity and love, who helped launch the psychology of wisdom by studying people's implicit theories of it and proposed the balance theory, which treats wisdom as using one's abilities for a common good.

title: Rumination
summary: The habit of repeatedly and passively turning over your distress, its causes and its consequences, without moving toward a solution or acceptance; it feels like thinking a problem through but tends to deepen low mood and stall action.
selfCheck: Has this round of thinking produced a new insight or a next step, or am I replaying the same scene?
Am I asking how to deal with this, or only why it happened and what it says about me?
What would I advise a friend in exactly this position, and can I take that advice tonight?
Have I tested the fear I keep circling, or only rehearsed it?

example.situation: In your annual review, your manager says your project updates are often late. That night you cannot stop thinking about it.
example.before: "Why do I always do this? What does she really think of me? I'm probably the weakest person on the team." Two hours later you are still replaying the meeting and have decided nothing.
example.after: "If a colleague told me this, I'd ask what exactly went wrong and what they'd do next. The last three updates slipped because I waited for complete data. I'll propose a short interim update every Friday and check that works for her." Then you put it down for the night.
example.why: Asking what happened and how to act, from a step back, turns the same worry into a plan, whereas asking why in a self-critical loop keeps the hurt fresh and leaves the problem untouched.

title: Seeking counsel
summary: Deliberately asking well-chosen people for their view before an important or uncertain decision, and then giving their advice real weight rather than only using it to confirm what you already think.
selfCheck: Did I ask people who know this kind of decision, or only people who would agree with me?
Did I ask without signalling the answer I wanted?
When the advice differed from my view, did I actually move, or did I explain it away?
Have I asked anyone who has already lived through this choice how it felt afterwards?
steps: Name the decision and decide whether it is important and uncertain enough to deserve outside counsel.
Write down your own current view and how confident you are, before you ask anyone.
Choose two or three advisers who know this kind of situation, including at least one who has lived through it and one likely to disagree with you.
Ask each one separately and personally, describe the problem without revealing your preferred answer, and ask what they would do and why.
Ask anyone who has already been through the same choice how it actually turned out and felt for them.
Compare their answers with your own and move your view meaningfully toward the advice where they know more or agree with each other, noting where and why you still differ.
Make the decision yourself, take responsibility for it, and later tell your advisers what you decided and how it went.

example.situation: A team lead has a job offer from a fast-growing start-up and must answer by Friday. They are excited and have already half-decided to accept.
example.before: I'll ask my best friend, who always backs me, mention the salary first, and take the yes as confirmation.
example.after: I'll write down my own answer first, then ask a former colleague who joined a start-up two years ago how it really went, and a mentor who tends to be cautious. I won't tell them which way I'm leaning, and I'll actually shift my view if they both raise the same worry.
example.why: Asking advisers who know the terrain, without steering them, gives the decision a second independent view and the lived experience of someone who has already been there, which people tend to undervalue.

title: Self-distancing
summary: Reflecting on your own feelings and problems from the vantage point of an outside observer, for example by picturing the scene as a "fly on the wall" or by silently addressing yourself by name or as "you", so that you can understand a difficult experience without being swept back into it.
selfCheck: Am I reliving this from the inside, or looking at it as an observer would?
Would I give a friend in my position the advice I am about to follow?
Have I asked what I might not know and how the other person sees this?
Is this distance helping me understand the feeling, or helping me avoid it?
steps: Notice the signs that you are immersed in an upsetting experience, such as replaying the same scene, rehearsing the same sentence or feeling the original anger or shame rise again.
Shift your vantage point by picturing the scene from across the room, as a neutral observer would see it, with yourself as one of the people in it.
Talk to yourself silently using your own name or "you" instead of "I", for example "Why is Sam so stung by this?"
Ask what lies behind the feeling and what you might be missing, rather than recounting again what happened.
Widen the frame by asking how the other people involved might see it, and how the situation could change over the coming months.
Ask what you would advise a friend in exactly this position, then choose one concrete next step.
Stop if the distance is turning into a way of avoiding the feeling or the problem, and seek support if the distress persists.

example.situation: Late on a Friday, your manager leaves a blunt comment on your project report saying the analysis "misses the point", and you feel your weekend souring.
example.before: I can't believe I got this so wrong. I'll keep rereading that comment, write a defensive reply tonight and hit send.
example.after: Why is Jordan so rattled by one line? Jordan doesn't yet know what the manager meant by 'the point'. If a friend showed me this, I'd tell them to ask one clarifying question on Monday, not to send a reply at midnight.
example.why: Viewing the moment as an observer cools the sting enough to admit what you don't know and to consider the other person's view, which is the kind of reasoning people find easier about a friend's problem than their own.

title: Socratic ignorance
aliases: knowing that one does not know
summary: The teaching, drawn from Plato's Apology, that the beginning of human wisdom is not thinking you know what you do not know: an honest awareness of the limits of your own understanding, especially about the most important questions of how to live.
selfCheck: Do I actually know this, or am I only confident about it?
If someone questioned me closely here, where would my account run out?
Am I treating skill in my own field as if it made me an authority on this question too?

example.situation: A team lead is asked in a planning meeting whether a new supplier can deliver on time, and has only skimmed their proposal.
example.before: Yes, they're solid, I'm sure of it. Let's lock them in.
example.after: I've only skimmed it, so I don't actually know. Here's what I'd need to check, and who has worked with them before?
example.why: Separating what you know from what you merely feel sure of keeps a confident guess from becoming the team's decision, and invites the people who do know to speak.

title: Solomon's paradox
summary: The tendency to reason more wisely about other people's problems than about our own: people facing a friend's conflict more readily admit what they do not know, seek compromise, weigh other viewpoints and expect change than they do when the same conflict is theirs.
selfCheck: If a friend brought me this exact problem, what would I tell them, and am I following that advice myself?
Could I state the other person's view in words they would accept as fair?
Have I admitted what I don't know about their motives and about how this could unfold?
Am I treating any compromise as a defeat?

example.situation: You recently helped a teammate think calmly through a clash with another department. This week a peer quietly reassigns part of your own project without asking you.
example.before: This is a power grab, plain and simple. I know exactly what they're up to, and I'm escalating to our director today.
example.after: If my teammate described this to me, I'd ask what they actually know about the peer's reasons, what a fair split could look like, and how it might look in a month. I'll ask the peer for ten minutes first.
example.why: Treating your own conflict as you would a colleague's brings back the habits you already use as an adviser, namely admitting what you don't know, looking for compromise and expecting the situation to change.

title: Stoicism
summary: A Hellenistic school of philosophy, founded in Athens around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium, which teaches that virtue is the only true good and that a flourishing life comes from living in agreement with nature and reason, judging wisely what is and is not up to us.

title: Susan Nolen-Hoeksema
summary: American clinical psychologist (1959–2013) at Stanford, Michigan and Yale who developed response styles theory and showed how rumination, passively dwelling on distress, deepens and prolongs depression and helps explain why women are more often depressed than men.
